tasks.locator: 3rd to 5th paragraphs; 9th and 10th paragraphs; Declaration of interests
tasks.extracted: An editorial by six authors summarizes Fillmore et al. (2006) as finding no significant protection in studies that kept former and occasional drinkers out of the abstainer group, describes Mendelian randomization as resembling a randomized trial more closely than traditional observational studies, and cites a genetic study in which drinkers carrying a variant linked to lower consumption had lower cardiovascular risk (Holmes et al., 2014). In the authors' stated opinion the protective hypothesis is so undermined that the field is due for repositioning; they recommend that burden-of-disease estimates and guidelines assume no protective effect and that guidelines discourage drinking for health reasons. Declaration of interests: none. Its summaries of other studies are second-hand. Editors' observation: three of its authors (Chikritzhs, Stockwell, Naimi) wrote the 2016 review.

tasks.locator: Results › Health risks associated with alcohol consumption, 2nd paragraph; Methods › Systematic review and meta-analysis, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Summary › Findings
tasks.extracted: The minimum of the DALY-weighted curve over all attributable outcomes (the theoretical minimum risk exposure level) was zero standard drinks a day (95% UI 0.0 to 0.8 drinks a day; the abstract prints the interval per week), and the weighted risk rose monotonically with intake; the protective associations for ischaemic heart disease and diabetes in females were offset by cancers, whose risk rose monotonically with intake. Weights were each outcome's global age-standardised DALY rate per 100,000 in 2016, both sexes; curves were fitted for 0 to 12.5 standard drinks a day; a covariate for former drinkers in the reference group was kept only for ischaemic heart disease, ischaemic stroke and diabetes. In a sensitivity analysis of the weights, the curve changed significantly only where diabetes and ischaemic heart disease made up more than 60% of deaths.

tasks.locator: Discussion, 7th and 8th paragraphs; Results, 8th paragraph; Summary › Funding
tasks.extracted: Citing a systematic review of Mendelian randomization studies (van de Luitgaarden et al., 2021), the discussion reports that 67% of such studies of cardiovascular disease and 75% of those of diabetes found no association with alcohol, and that only five of 24 tested a non-linear relationship. Stated limitations: drinking patterns not modelled; alcohol use disorders excluded from the TMREL; possible residual confounding, selection bias, measurement bias and reverse causation in the relative risks; self-reported intake; weights that include DALYs caused by alcohol; depression, anxiety and dementia not included, which would possibly lower the TMREL and NDE. Hypothetical curves for alcohol use disorders and alcoholic cardiomyopathy lowered the TMREL on average by 0.058 (0.00 to 0.30), 0.092 (0.00 to 0.50) and 0.146 (0.00 to 0.60) standard drinks a day in three scenarios. Funded by the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation.
